analysis.one_liner: Repeals corporate, estate, and gift taxes and taxes only wages above $10,000 at 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed every corporate and estate tax and taxed only wages above $10,000 at a flat 10%, never got a hearing or a vote, ending with 4 cosponsors when the Congress expired.
analysis.plain_summary: The Crane Tithe Tax Act would have eliminated the corporate income tax and a dozen related business taxes, repealed the estate and gift taxes, and forgiven all unpaid income tax debt from before 1988. In their place, it would have taxed only wages and self-employment income above $10,000 at a flat 10% — meaning income from investments, such as interest, dividends, capital gains, and rents, would have been taxed at zero. It would also have wiped out every individual tax deduction and credit, including the mortgage interest deduction and the Earned Income Tax Credit.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households living on investment income gain the most: under this bill, only earned income (wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings) is taxed, so interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, and royalties would be tax-free [S2][S3]. Corporations gain because the corporate income tax, the corporate alternative minimum tax, and special taxes on insurance companies, mutual savings banks, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, foreign corporations, and even tax-exempt organizations' business income would all be repealed [S2][S3]. Wealthy families gain because the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes on passing large fortunes to heirs — would be abolished [S2][S3]. Anyone with unpaid federal income tax from before 1988 would have that debt, plus penalties and interest, wiped clean (except for income from illegal activity) [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax and eleven related taxes, including taxes on insurance companies, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, foreign corporations' U.S. income, and the business income of tax-exempt organizations, so corporations and investment vehicles would owe no federal income tax.
Abolishes the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, so large fortunes could pass to heirs untaxed.
Taxes only 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings — at 10% above a $10,000 exemption, leaving interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, and royalties entirely untaxed.
Declares tax amnesty for all pre-1988 income tax liability, canceling unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest for anyone who had not paid (except income from illegal activity).

analysis.who_pays: Working people would bear the cost. Wages and salaries would be the only meaningful tax base left: everyone earning above the $10,000 exemption pays 10% of the excess, with every deduction and credit repealed — including the mortgage interest deduction, child-related credits, and the Earned Income Tax Credit that supplements low-wage work [S2][S3]. Meanwhile the bill repeals the corporate income tax, estate tax, and gift tax without replacing that revenue, so the burden of funding the government shifts onto paychecks — either through larger deficits or future tax increases on workers. Pensioners and people living off investments would owe nothing [S3]. People who paid their taxes before 1988 get nothing back, while those who dodged get forgiveness [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing all individual deductions, exclusions, and credits would end the mortgage interest deduction, child-related credits, and the Earned Income Tax Credit, which directly reduces take-home pay and support for low- and middle-income working families.

The bill raises money only from a 10% tax on wages above $10,000 while repealing the corporate income tax, estate tax, gift tax, and a dozen business taxes, so federal revenue would fall far short of spending — meaning either large deficits or future tax increases falling on workers.
The amnesty cancels all pre-1988 income tax debt, penalties, and interest, letting people who never paid their taxes off the hook while everyone who paid receives nothing.

Because investment income, pensions, and annuities are excluded from tax, a retiree or a wealthy person living off dividends and capital gains would owe nothing, while a worker earning the same total income would pay 10% on everything above $10,000.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is simplicity — a single 10% rate and no deductions would make filing easy — but that simplicity comes at an enormous cost in fairness. It would concentrate the entire income tax on wages, exempt all investment and inherited wealth from tax, and hand corporations and estates a full repeal of their taxes with no replacement revenue. Even a supporter who valued flat-tax simplicity would have to acknowledge that the burden shift onto working paychecks and the unpaid pre-1988 tax debt forgiven are fundamental, not incidental, features of the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing committee on day one and sat there, with no hearing, no vote, and no action of any kind, until that Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Representative Philip Crane introduced the Crane Tithe Tax Act on January 4, 1989, the opening day of the 101st Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day; that referral was the only action the bill ever received.
Four House Republicans cosponsored the bill, all from Crane's own party; no Democrat signed on.
The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary wage earners are better off because the bill died: the existing progressive income tax with its deductions and credits, the corporate income tax, and the estate tax all remained in place, and no one received the pre-1988 tax amnesty.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners who use deductions and credits

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 101st Congress.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the Democrat-controlled Ways and Means Committee never moved the bill, so the small amount of visible support ran entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and the corporate alternative minimum tax outright, so corporations would pay no federal income tax; the lost revenue would fall on wage earners instead.
Investment income, pensions, and inheritances would go untaxed, while the estate and gift taxes on passing wealth to heirs are repealed — the bill's entire remaining tax base is wages.
The special federal taxes on life, mutual, and other insurance companies (sections 801, 821, and 831) would be repealed entirely.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The taxes on regulated investment companies and REITs (sections 852 and 857) would be repealed, removing federal income tax from these investment vehicles.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would shrink demand for estate-tax avoidance planning even as their wealthy clients' wealth transfers became tax-free.
The unrelated business income tax on tax-exempt organizations' commercial ventures would be repealed, letting nonprofits run businesses tax-free.
